GitLab for the model team

How a government model team runs a SysML v1 → v2 port, and the model's maintenance afterwards, in GitLab: the features, why each one is worth the trouble, the scripts that set them up, and filled-in samples of every text field.

Who this is for

This guide is for systems engineers who have done configuration management for years, with documents, spreadsheets, briefings and, lately, a Cameo model, and who have now been told to "do DevSecOps". If that model turned into a spider web that nobody could review, and the new direction feels like one more tool on top, this guide is for you.

Three things to know before you start:

  • Most of DevSecOps is configuration management you already know, done in smaller pieces and checked by machine. A merge request is a change request. An approval is a CCB signature. The pipeline is a configuration audit. A protected tag is a baseline. The glossary translates every term.
  • Each section below starts with "Why bother": the objection a seasoned engineer raises (because the old way worked, or seemed to), and what the feature gives back for the effort.
  • Every new word is defined the first time it appears, and again in the glossary.
Why bother at all? The documents-and-briefings way scaled with people: every review, audit and status chart was somebody's week. The Cameo model added a tool without changing that, and grew into a web nobody could review. Here the model is plain text, split into owned pieces; every change is small, shown line by line, reviewed, and audited by machine before it reaches the master copy; and status comes out of the work itself. The effort moves from chasing to doing.
The running example is Tidewater, a fictional coastal weather-observation network. The prime contractor (the fictional Northwind Marine Systems) keeps the authoritative SysML v1 model in Cameo and the requirements in DOORS, and delivers them as drops. The government team ports each drop to SysML v2 text in a GitLab project and keeps it current: Jim, the MBSE lead responsible for the model, directed this year to follow DevSecOps for the first time; Bob, the MBSE engineer; and Tom, the configuration management engineer, who also runs the pipeline. None of them had done DevSecOps before. Every name and value is notional. The simulation of 18 months of that work is in sim/tidewater-sim.pl; the walk-through of its first 12 weeks is TIDEWATER.html.

What GitLab does, in terms you know

GitLab is a web server that holds the model's files under version control (a repository: every file, with every change ever made to it) and the work around them: change requests, reviews, audits, action items, baselines. Each feature below carries one job you already do. The table is the map; the sections after it are the detail. GitLab is sold in tiers: Free, Premium and Ultimate; the last column says which one a feature needs.

You have always neededGitLab featureHow Tidewater uses itTier
One place for the model, its history and who changed whatProject (Git repository)tidewater/model; SysML v2 text under model/Free
Released baselines that never changeProtected branch main, protected tags baseline-*, ReleasesA baseline is a merge to main, a tag and a release with notesFree
Integration without breaking the modelProtected branch develop, merge requests, pipelines must succeedEvery change arrives by MR; the gate is lint 0/0Free
The prime's changes merged with oursA protected vendor branch and Git's three-way mergevendor/prime holds raw converter output of each dropFree
The right person reviews each partCODEOWNERS, approval rulesBob owns structure, Jim owns requirements, Tom owns the pipelinePremium (enforced); Free shows owners
Checks nobody can skipCI/CD pipelines, merge checksgrammar, lint, outline, secrets, trace, docs, delta, baselineFree
SprintsMilestones (Free) or iterations (Premium)Sprint 1 … Sprint 39, two weeks eachFree
Stories and tasksIssues and tasks, templates, quick actionsStory and task issues; "Part of #N"Free
Epics and tomesGroup epics, multi-level epics (Premium/Ultimate) or labels (Free)epic::* and tome::* labelsFree (labels)
Work visible at a glanceIssue boards with label listsThe Sprint and Prime boardsFree
Mutually exclusive statesScoped labels (workflow::ready)One workflow, type and priority per issuePremium (Free: the names still work, not exclusive)

Which GitLab DevSecOps tools this team uses, and why

The objection: "GitLab has hundreds of features. We are three people with a model to port; we cannot learn all of that." Why bother: you should not learn all of it. The table below is the short list worth the set-up time for a three-person model team, each with the job it takes off your hands. Everything else is deliberately left off, and the second table says why, so nobody feels they are missing something.

Tiers are as of GitLab 17. Check your instance's edition (Help > Help shows it); where a feature needs a tier you do not have, the "Set up" column gives the Free-tier way.

FeatureTierValue for a 3-person MBSE teamSet up
Issue boardsFreeThe action-item tracker everybody sees, with no spreadsheet to update: moving a card changes its status[labels] in project.conf; Plan > Issue boards, one list per workflow:: label
Scoped labels (key::value)PremiumAn item has exactly one status, type and priority; no "in progress and done" cardsName labels key::value (setup does). On Free, the names still work; remove the old one yourself
Milestones as sprintsFreeThe two-week time box and its list of work, in one place[milestones] sprints = 2026-10-05 39 2
Burndown and burnup chartsPremiumThe sprint's progress drawn for you on the milestone pageNothing: they appear on each milestone. On Free, use the journal's sprint report
Time tracking (/estimate, /spend)FreeSizes tasks in days, keeping the "under a week" rule visible; actuals for the next estimateUse the quick actions; templates include /estimate
CODEOWNERSFree (shown) / Premium (enforced)The CCB, per package: the right person approves each part of the modelCommit CODEOWNERS; codeowners:yes under [branches]
Approval rulesPremiumA minimum number of approvals on every change, and no self-approval[approvals] Model review = 1 jim bob; Settings > Merge requests: prevent approval by author
Protected branches and tagsFreeNobody changes the master copy or a baseline except through an approved change[branches], [tags]
Push rulesPremiumThe server rejects commits with no issue reference, files that should never be committed (exports, .mdzip), and secretsSettings > Repository > Push rules: commit message regex #\d+, file name deny list \.(mdzip|exe)$, prevent secrets

EnvironmentsFreeRecords which commit the published site shows, and when it changedenvironment: model-site on the pages job
ReleasesFreeEach baseline with its notes and evidence, on one page that lists every baselineThe publish-release job on baseline-* tags
Package registry (generic)FreeEach prime drop kept exactly as delivered, by version, beside the model it became: the CDRL recordThe drop-package job; nothing to configure (the job token authenticates)
Scheduled pipelinesFreeThe weekly status computed on Monday morning, with no one typing it upBuild > Pipeline schedules, Mondays 06:00; variable STATUS_TOKEN
Audit eventsPremiumWho changed a protection, a member or a token, and when: the CM office's access logSecure > Audit events; review monthly
Value stream analyticsFree (project) / Premium (custom stages)How long work takes from issue to merge, so the team sees where it waitsAnalyze > Value stream analytics; nothing to set up
DORA metricsUltimateChange frequency, lead time, failure rate and restore time, computed from the model-site environmentAnalyze > CI/CD analytics; mark model-site as a production-tier environment
WikiFreeThe process, the definitions and the decisions, versioned like the modelgitlab.pl wiki put each page from templates/wiki/

The work hierarchy in GitLab

The objection: "We have a WBS and an IMS. Why tomes, epics, stories and tasks?" Why bother: they are a WBS, sized by time instead of by contract line, so you always know how far away "done" is. A task that takes more than a week is a task nobody can see the end of; splitting it is how the team finds the hidden work early, while there is still time.

The team sizes work by time, from the biggest to the smallest. One point is one ideal person-day.

LevelSize limitTidewater exampleGitLab FreeGitLab Premium / UltimateAgile kit journal
ProjectyearsThe v1 → v2 port and maintenance, 18 monthsthe group tidewaterthe groupone journal: data/tidewater/journal
Tomeunder 1 year (2 semesters)Port Tidewater v1 to SysML v2label tome::porttop-level epic (Ultimate: multi-level)t: on each story
Epicunder 1 semester (13 sprints)Structure portissue type::epic + label epic::structuregroup epice: on each story
Storyunder 1 sprintClose the Stations TODO linesissue type::story in milestone Sprint 4issue in an iterationan item TW-<issue>
Taskunder 1 week (≤ 5 points)Write state def BuoyModesissue type::task, "Part of #18"task (child work item)not recorded: task detail stays in GitLab

The split between GitLab and the journal follows the kit's ownership rule: the architect's journal records stories, epics and tomes (what the program steers by); tasks and hours stay in the team's own tool. A story's journal id is its GitLab issue number, so TW-18 in a stand-up is #18 in GitLab.

On Free, an epic is an ordinary issue carrying type::epic, plus a label its stories carry. The epic issue's task list (- [ ] #18) shows progress as "3 of 7 checklist items". On Premium, move the text into a group epic and attach the stories; nothing else in the process changes.

Setting up the project

The objection: "Somebody clicks through the settings once and we are done." Why bother: the settings are the configuration control rules: who may change the master copy, who approves, what is audited. Kept in a file, they are reviewed, versioned and re-applied like any controlled document, and you can prove at any time that the server still matches them.

A project is a set of settings as much as a repository. bin/gitlab.pl setup applies them from one file, so they are reviewed like code, rebuilt in minutes, and compared with the server at any time. Re-running it is safe: it creates what is missing and updates what differs.

# against the real server: a token with the api scope, in an environment variable
export GITLAB_TOKEN=...                       # never on the command line, never in a file in the repo
perl bin/gitlab.pl --url https://gitlab.example.com --token-env GITLAB_TOKEN --dry-run setup tools/gitlab/templates/project.conf
perl bin/gitlab.pl --url https://gitlab.example.com --token-env GITLAB_TOKEN setup tools/gitlab/templates/project.conf

# offline: the same commands against the emulator (a directory)
perl bin/gitlab.pl --local data/tidewater/gitlab setup tools/gitlab/templates/project.conf
perl bin/gitlab.pl --local data/tidewater/gitlab --project tidewater/model sprints 2026-10-05 39

--dry-run prints every API call it would make and changes nothing; read it the first time. The offline emulator (--local DIR) keeps the project state in DIR/gitlab.json and the repository as a bare Git repo, with a server-side hook that enforces the branch and tag protections. It is how this kit tests the scripts and runs the simulation, and how you can rehearse a change to the settings before applying it.

The project file for Tidewater. Lines are key = value; a ; starts a comment (not #, which label colours use):

# project.conf -- the Tidewater model project, as `gitlab.pl setup` applies it (tools/gitlab/templates/project.conf).
#
#   perl bin/gitlab.pl --url https://gitlab.example.com --token-env GITLAB_TOKEN setup tools/gitlab/templates/project.conf
#   perl bin/gitlab.pl --local data/tidewater/gitlab setup tools/gitlab/templates/project.conf      (the offline emulator)
#
# Every setting here is something a maintainer would otherwise click through in Settings. Keeping it in a file means the
# project can be rebuilt, reviewed in a merge request, and compared with what the server actually has. Re-running setup
# is safe: it creates what is missing and updates what differs.
# Tidewater is fictional; the people are Jim (MBSE lead, responsible for the model), Bob (MBSE engineer) and Tom
# (configuration management engineer, who also runs the pipeline). None of them had done DevSecOps before this year.

[project]
path = tidewater/model
default_branch = develop                                  ; gitflow: develop is where work lands, so issues close there
merge_method = merge                                      ; a merge commit for every MR: the metrics read merge history
squash_option = never                                     ; keep each commit; squash would hide who changed what
only_allow_merge_if_pipeline_succeeds = true
only_allow_merge_if_all_discussions_are_resolved = true
remove_source_branch_after_merge = true
visibility = private

[members]
jim = maintainer                                          ; MBSE lead: owns tomes, epics, baselines and releases
bob = developer                                           ; MBSE engineer: ports and maintains the model
tom = maintainer                                          ; CM: pipeline, runners, vendor branch, tags

[branches]
main = push:none merge:maintainer force:no codeowners:yes          ; released baselines only, through release/hotfix MRs
develop = push:none merge:developer force:no codeowners:yes        ; integration; every change arrives by MR
release/* = push:maintainer merge:maintainer force:no
hotfix/* = push:maintainer merge:maintainer force:no
vendor/prime = push:maintainer merge:none force:no                 ; raw converter output of each prime drop, never hand-edited

[tags]
baseline-* = create:maintainer                            ; a baseline is permanent: nobody can move or delete it

[labels]
; type -- what kind of work item it is (scoped: an issue has exactly one type)
type::epic = #5843AD | A collection of stories finished within one semester (13 sprints)
type::story = #428BCA | A slice of value of several tasks that fits in one sprint
type::task = #69D100 | One piece of work under a story, less than a week (5 points or fewer)
type::defect = #D9534F | Something in the government v2 model or pipeline is wrong
type::discrepancy = #AD4363 | A problem in the prime's v1 model or DOORS, reported to the prime (Discrepancy Report)
type::drop = #00B140 | Intake of one prime model drop (XMI + ReqIF + CSV under CDRL A003)
type::spike = #8E44AD | Time-boxed investigation that ends in a decision, not a model change
; tome -- the year-scale grouping (< 2 semesters)
tome::T1-stand-up = #36454F | T1 Stand up MBSE DevSecOps (sprints 1-8)
tome::T2-port = #36454F | T2 Port Tidewater v1 to SysML v2 (sprints 1-20)
tome::T3-maintain = #36454F | T3 Maintain against prime drops (sprints 17-39)

epic::E1-gitlab = #6699CC | E1 GitLab project and gitflow
epic::E2-pipeline = #6699CC | E2 Pipeline and quality gates
epic::E3-practices = #6699CC | E3 Team practices and onboarding
epic::E4-toolchain-security = #6699CC | E4 Toolchain security and authorization to use
epic::E5-drop-1 = #6699CC | E5 Drop 1 intake and first import
epic::E6-structure = #6699CC | E6 Structure: close the structure TODOs
epic::E7-requirements = #6699CC | E7 Requirements and trace
epic::E8-behavior = #6699CC | E8 Behavior and analysis
epic::E9-drops-2-3 = #6699CC | E9 Drops 2 and 3 during the port
epic::E10-baseline-1 = #6699CC | E10 Baseline 1 and acceptance
epic::E11-intake-automation = #6699CC | E11 Drop intake automation
epic::E12-drops-4-5 = #6699CC | E12 Drops 4 and 5
epic::E13-drops-6-7 = #6699CC | E13 Drops 6 and 7
epic::E14-sustainment = #6699CC | E14 Sustainment operations
; workflow -- where the item is on the board (scoped: moving it replaces the old one)
workflow::ready = #A8D695 | Meets the Definition of Ready; can be pulled into a sprint
workflow::in-progress = #F0AD4E | Someone is working it
workflow::review = #F0AD4E | An MR is open and waiting for review or approval
workflow::blocked = #D9534F | Cannot move; the blocker is in the latest comment
workflow::done = #5CB85C | Meets the Definition of Done
; priority, severity, owner, phase
priority::1 = #CC0033 | Do first
priority::2 = #FC9403 | Normal
priority::3 = #C0C0C0 | When there is room
severity::1 = #CC0033 | Wrong model content that would mislead an analysis
severity::2 = #FC9403 | Wrong or missing content with a workaround
severity::3 = #C0C0C0 | Cosmetic
owner::gov = #1F3A5F | The government team fixes it
owner::prime = #B8860B | The prime fixes it in a later drop
phase::port = #7F8C8D | Found or done during the port
phase::maintenance = #7F8C8D | Found or done after baseline 1
phase::integration = #7F8C8D | Found when parts were brought together
; area -- which model package it touches (one per top-level package; CODEOWNERS uses the same split)
area::network = #E0E0E0 | model/physical/network
area::stations = #E0E0E0 | model/physical/stations
area::datacenter = #E0E0E0 | model/physical/datacenter
area::operations = #E0E0E0 | model/physical/operations
area::interfaces = #E0E0E0 | model/library/Interfaces.sysml
area::interface = #E0E0E0 | A defect at an interface between packages (status metric H counts these)
area::types = #E0E0E0 | model/library/Types.sysml
area::analysis = #E0E0E0 | model/analysis
area::behavior = #E0E0E0 | model/logical
area::allocations = #E0E0E0 | model/physical/allocation
area::requirements = #E0E0E0 | model/requirements (the three DOORS modules and the Cameo copy)
area::verification = #E0E0E0 | model/verification and verification/*.csv (results)
area::legacy = #E0E0E0 | model/legacy (clutter from the document port; removed upstream in drop 6)
area::pipeline = #E0E0E0 | .gitlab-ci.yml, ci/job.pl, runners, the kit
area::gov = #E0E0E0 | government additions (model/library/conventions, model/logical/GovBehavior.sysml)
; doc -- the review stage of a document issue: the Document Review Stages scale, Grey (collection) to Green (releasable), with percent and grade bands; scoped
doc::grey = #A0A0A0 | Grey, Collection (1-24%, G- to G+): a loose collection of content, started
doc::blue = #4A90D9 | Blue, Compliant (25-45%, F- to F+): the outline is complete
doc::pink = #E89AC7 | Pink, Complete (46-63%, D- to D+): content stable and consistent throughout
doc::red = #D9534F | Red, Compelling (64-78%, C- to C+): graphics, tables, data, spelling, acronyms and grammar finalized
doc::gold = #D4AF37 | Gold, Comprehensive (79-90%, B- to B+): sound, coherent and actionable
doc::white = #F5F5F5 | White, Copy Ready (91-99%, A- to A+): ready for hard-copy review
doc::green = #5CB85C | Green, Done (100%): releasable
; prime changes -- each significant item of a prime drop's delta, dispositioned by Jim and the deputy PM (the CCB)
prime-change = #B8860B | One significant change the prime made in a drop (cite the prime's CR id, NWM-CR-nnnn)
prime-tbd = #B8860B | Work that rests on an assumption about the prime's next drop; closed when the drop lands
disposition::accept = #5CB85C | Accepted as delivered
disposition::accept-with-impact = #F0AD4E | Accepted; it adds government work (tasks linked), cost and schedule noted
disposition::reject-clarify = #D9534F | Not accepted yet: a DR asks the prime for the rationale
disposition::no-impact = #C0C0C0 | Cosmetic: nothing for the government model to do
work::engineering = #1F77B4 | Systems engineering with the model: the reason the platform exists
work::platform = #7F7F7F | The platform: GitLab, the pipeline, runners, tokens, templates
work::learning = #2CA02C | Time to learn the tools and the way of working (planned, not stolen from evenings)
ai::assisted = #8E44AD | an MR whose first draft came from the local SysML assistant (measured: first-pipeline pass rate)

[milestones]
sprints = 2026-10-05 39 2                                 ; Sprint 1 .. Sprint 39, two weeks each, 18 months

[approvals]
Model review = 1 jim bob                                  ; one of Jim or Bob approves every MR (Premium; enforced locally)

[variables]
KIT = /opt/agile                                          ; where the runner has the kit checked out (the jobs call $KIT/...)
DOCKER_RUNNER = false                                     ; "true" only on a Docker-executor runner: pulls in GitLab's Secret-Detection template

[schedules]
; Description = CRON | REF | TIME ZONE | KEY=VALUE ...   (CI/CD > Schedules; the pipeline sees $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule")
; Cron is minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, read in the time zone given (US daylight saving included).
; The schedule's owner is whoever runs setup: it runs as them, so use a maintainer who will stay on the project.
Nightly full check = 0 2 * * 1-5 | develop | America/New_York | FULL=1   ; weeknights 02:00 Eastern: every job, uncached
Weekly status = 0 6 * * 5 | develop | America/New_York                  ; Friday 06:00 Eastern: export + status metrics for the weekly report

[labels]
; where a request came from (scoped); a second [labels] section adds to the first
source::windchill = #3E6E8E | A request submitted in Windchill; the Windchill number starts the title (gitlab.pl windchill intake)

[boards]
; NAME = LABEL LABEL ... | milestone=started|upcoming|none|any|TITLE | iteration=current|any|none | sprint=current
; (Plan > Issue boards; one list per label, in order). Scoping a board is Premium/Ultimate (the norm on GitLab Dedicated);
; on Free setup warns and the board shows everything. sprint=current follows the sprint that is running, so the board
; never needs editing at a sprint change: the started milestone, or the current iteration when [iterations] use = iterations.
Sprint = workflow::ready workflow::in-progress workflow::review workflow::blocked workflow::done | sprint=current
Backlog = priority::1 priority::2 priority::3 | milestone=none          ; refinement: what no sprint holds yet, by priority

[iterations]
; GitLab's own sprints (Premium/Ultimate): an iteration cadence makes a two-week iteration after another by itself.
; Cadences live on the GROUP, not the project, and GitLab changes them only through GraphQL: setup needs the group path
; and Maintainer on that group. [milestones] above stay the fallback; `use` decides what sprint=current and
; `gitlab.pl analytics --by sprint` mean. Tidewater keeps milestones; to switch, uncomment the cadence and set use.
use = milestones                                          ; milestones (the sprints above) or iterations (the cadence)
; group = tidewater                                       ; the group the cadence lives on (default: the project's namespace)
; Sprints = 2026-10-05 2 4 | automatic                    ; TITLE = START WEEKS IN_ADVANCE [| automatic roll-over manual]

[insights]
; Analyze > Insights (Ultimate) draws the charts in .gitlab/insights.yml on the default branch. setup generates the file
; from the labels here (workflow::, severity::, work::, the Windchill source label) and writes it into the repository when
; it runs on the repository's .gitlab/project.conf; commit it through a merge request (or setup --commit opens one).
; gitlab.pl insights prints it. Insights groups by week or month, not by sprint.
file = .gitlab/insights.yml
weeks = 12                                                ; how many weeks each chart shows

[windchill]
; Requests arrive in Windchill; the team works them in GitLab. gitlab.pl windchill intake EXPORT.csv makes one issue per
; new Windchill number from a report exported as CSV; gitlab.pl windchill status --csv FILE is the progress to send back.
; Column names as the export's header has them (Windchill report or search-result export; adjust to yours):
number = Number
title = Name
state = State
type = Type
requester = Created By
priority = Priority
need-date = Need Date
description = Description
url = https://windchill.example.invalid/Windchill/app/#ptc1/search?keyword={number}   ; the link in each issue
labels = source::windchill, type::story                   ; added to every issue made from a request
accept = Open, Under Review, Approved                     ; states imported; the others are reported as skipped (* = all)
priority-map = Critical=priority::1, High=priority::1, Medium=priority::2, Low=priority::3

The order, the first time

Protecting main with push:none also stops the very first push, so the skeleton goes in before the protections:

  1. Create an empty project tidewater/model (New project > Create blank project, without a README), or let setup create it from a copy of the file that holds only [project].
  2. Push the skeleton to main and create develop: 
    git clone https://gitlab.example.com/tidewater/model.git && cd model
cp $KIT/tools/gitlab/templates/gitlab-ci.yml .gitlab-ci.yml
cp $KIT/tools/gitlab/templates/{CODEOWNERS,README.md,CHANGELOG.md} .
cp -r $KIT/tools/gitlab/templates/.gitlab .
git add -A && git commit -m "Project skeleton: pipeline, templates, owners" && git push -u origin main
perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl flow init            # develop from main, pushed
  3. Apply the whole file: gitlab.pl setup project.conf. From here on main and develop take changes only by merge request, and develop is the default branch.
  4. Register a runner (Administration) and check that the CI/CD variable KIT points at the kit's checkout on it.
  5. Create the weekly pipeline schedule (Build > Pipeline schedules, Mondays 06:00) and a masked CI/CD variable STATUS_TOKEN holding a read_api project access token.
  6. Put the wiki pages from tools/gitlab/templates/wiki/, one command per page: gitlab.pl wiki put "Definition of Done" "templates/wiki/Definition of Done.md".

Gitflow

The objection: "We had one master copy and it worked." Why bother: you still have one master copy (develop). Branches are the working copies everyone always made anyway, on their own drives and in e-mail attachments, except that Git knows about them and can bring the changes back in exactly. The baselines get their own branch (main) so a release never waits on, or is disturbed by, the work in progress.

The model is released: analyses and reviews cite a baseline, and a baseline must never change. Day-to-day work must never wait on a release either. Gitflow gives each its own branch: main is exactly the list of baselines, develop is where the work integrates, and short-lived branches carry each change. Tidewater adds one branch gitflow does not have, vendor/prime, for the prime's drops.

BranchCreated fromMerges intoWho pushesWho mergesLifetime
main(the first commit)—nobodymaintainers: Jim, Tomforever; baselines only
developmain—nobodydevelopers, after approvalforever; the default branch
feature/<iid>-<slug>developdevelopits author—one task or story; deleted on merge
release/baseline-Ndevelopmain (then back-merge)maintainersmaintainersdays
hotfix/<name>mainmain and developmaintainersmaintainershours
vendor/primethe first commit of maindevelop, through feature/drop-<version>Tom onlynobodyforever; never edited by hand

Rules the team keeps

  • Name feature branches after the issue: feature/19-stations-level-tags. GitLab links the branch to issue 19, and the MR gets "Closes #19" from the template.
  • Merge commits, never squash or rebase-merge. The merge history is evidence: who changed which package when, how long an MR was open, how many merges needed a fix-forward. The status metrics read it.
  • develop is the default branch. GitLab closes issues named by "Closes #N" only when the MR merges into the default branch; with gitflow that is develop.
  • A feature branch lives less than a week, like the task it carries. Longer branches drift from the prime's drops and conflict.
  • Releases and hotfixes back-merge into develop the same day, so a fix is never lost.

The commands

gitlab.pl flow does the branch bookkeeping and opens the merge requests, from the current clone:

perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl flow start feature 19-stations-level-tags   # from an up-to-date develop
# ... edit, commit ...
perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl flow publish                                 # push, and the MR pipeline starts once the MR exists
perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl flow finish --title "Replace the Stations level-tag TODOs" \
     --template .gitlab/merge_request_templates/Default.md          # MR to develop

perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl flow start release baseline-1                # from develop
perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl flow finish --template .gitlab/merge_request_templates/Release.md   # MR to main;
#   after it merges: tag baseline-1, release, back-merge MR main -> develop

perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl flow start hotfix cell-level-tag             # from main
perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl flow sync                                    # fetch; fast-forward develop and main

The same with plain Git, for when you want to see each step:

git switch develop && git pull --ff-only
git switch -c feature/19-stations-level-tags
git commit -am "Replace the Stations level-tag TODOs with @L tags" -m "Changelog: changed" -m "Issue: #19"
git push -u origin feature/19-stations-level-tags \
    -o merge_request.create -o merge_request.target=develop \
    -o merge_request.title="Replace the Stations level-tag TODOs" -o merge_request.label="workflow::review"

The -o merge_request.* push options make GitLab open the MR as part of the push, with no token and no web page. They are a quick alternative to flow finish, without the template.

Protected branches and tags

The objection: "We trust our people." Why bother: protection is not about trust; it is about accidents. One stray save into the master copy, one baseline overwritten, used to cost a week of reconstruction. Here the server refuses it, for everyone including the project lead, so nobody has to remember the rule.

Protection is what turns the branch table above from a convention into a rule. Settings > Repository > Protected branches and Protected tags; gitlab.pl setup applies the [branches] and [tags] sections.

SettingValue for main / developWhat it prevents
Allowed to push and mergeNo one (push); maintainers / developers (merge)A change that skipped review and the pipeline
Allowed to force pushoffRewriting history that baselines, MRs and metrics point at
Require approval from code ownersonA package changing without its owner seeing it (Premium)
Protected tag baseline-*, allowed to createmaintainersA baseline created, moved or deleted by mistake: protected tags cannot be updated or deleted from Git
Pipelines must succeed (merge checks)onA merge with a red or missing pipeline
All threads must be resolvedonA merge with an open review question

In the offline emulator the same rules live in a pre-receive hook in the bare repository. A direct push to develop is refused the same way GitLab refuses it:

remote: GitLab: You are not allowed to push code to protected branches on this project.
 ! [remote rejected] develop -> develop (pre-receive hook declined)

Code owners and approvals

The objection: "The CCB meets monthly; that is our approval." Why bother: a monthly board batches a month of changes into one meeting nobody can fully read. Code owners are the CCB split by package and available every day: each change is small enough to read in minutes, and it is approved by the person who knows that part of the model. The monthly board can then review baselines and decisions instead of redlines.

CODEOWNERS says who must approve a change to which path. GitLab reads it from the MR's target branch, so a change to the file itself only takes effect once it is merged. Sections let one MR need approvals from several owners: a change to Stations and to the requirements needs Bob or Jim and Jim.

# CODEOWNERS -- who must approve a change to which part of the Tidewater model repo.
# GitLab reads this file from the MR's TARGET branch (CODEOWNERS, docs/CODEOWNERS or .gitlab/CODEOWNERS, first found).
# With "code owner approval" on a protected branch (project.conf [branches] codeowners:yes), an MR that touches a path
# below needs an approval from one of that path's owners. The last matching pattern in a section wins.
#
# Sections group the rules; each section is checked on its own, so one MR can need an approval from several sections.
# [Name][2] would require two approvals from that section; ^[Name] makes a section optional (advisory only).

# Every section names at least two owners: GitLab never lets an author approve their own MR, so a section whose only
# owner wrote the change could never be satisfied. The model folders are the layers of the layout map
# (examples/tidewater-v1/layout.map): library -> requirements -> logical -> physical -> analysis -> verification.
[Pipeline and repository] @tom @jim
/.gitlab-ci.yml
/ci/
/.ci/
/.gitlab/
/.gitignore
/.kit-version
/CODEOWNERS             @tom @jim
/sysml.conf             @tom @bob

# Decisions: Jim records them, Bob (or Tom) reviews.
[Decisions] @jim @bob
/docs/adr/

[Library and conventions] @bob @jim
/model/library/

# Interfaces are where segments meet, so an interface change needs TWO approvals: the systems lead's (Jim decides every
# interface; Jim does not author interface changes) and one of the people who build on both sides (Bob or Tom,
# whoever did not write the change). Two sections, each must be satisfied.
[Systems lead] @jim
/model/library/Interfaces.sysml

[Interfaces] @bob @tom
/model/library/Interfaces.sysml

# Requirements belong to the government: Jim approves every change to them, from either converter (Bob when Jim wrote it).
[Requirements and verification] @jim @bob
/model/requirements/
/model/verification/
/verification/

[Logical and physical] @bob @jim
/model/logical/
/model/physical/
/model/legacy/

[Analysis] @jim @bob
/model/analysis/

# Raw prime drops arrive through vendor/prime; Tom imports them, Jim accepts them.
[Prime drops] @tom @jim
/imports/

# Generated docs: whoever changed the model regenerates them; advisory only.
^[Generated docs] @bob @tom
/docs/
On GitLab Free the owners are shown on each file and MR, but "require approval from code owners" and approval rules need Premium. On Free, the team keeps the rule by convention: the MR template assigns the reviewer, and the merge is done by someone other than the author.

Approval rules (Premium) add a project-wide minimum on top: Model review = 1 jim bob means one approval from Jim or Bob on every MR. Set Prevent approval by author and Remove all approvals when commits are added to the source branch under Settings > Merge requests.

Merge requests

The objection: "An ECP takes weeks; this sounds like more paperwork." Why bother: a merge request is the change request, the redlines, the review comments, the audit results and the approval signature in one page that writes itself from the work. It is less paperwork, not more: nobody assembles a package, and the record cannot be lost or backdated.
  1. Open it early as a draft (Draft: title prefix, or /draft). The pipeline runs on every push, and the reviewer can follow along.
  2. Fill the template. Default for a task, Prime Drop for a drop merge, Release and Hotfix for those branches. The template carries "Closes #N", the checks list, and quick actions that set the label and reviewer.
  3. The pipeline runs on the merged result: the source merged into the current target, the commit that would exist after the merge (Premium calls this merged results pipelines; the emulator always does it).
  4. Review in threads. Comment on a line; propose a change with a suggestion block the author applies with one click; resolve each thread when it is answered.
  5. Approve, then merge. The merge checks are: not a draft, pipeline succeeded, threads resolved, approvals met (code owners included). GitLab writes the merge commit as Merge branch 'feature/19-…' into 'develop', with the title, "Closes #19" and "See merge request tidewater/model!19".

A filled-in MR description and its review thread are in Markdown, field by field.

CI/CD from zero

The objection: "CI/CD is for software. We build models and documents." Why bother: strip the software words away and CI/CD is two habits a configuration manager already values. One is checking every change the day it is made. The other is keeping the deliverables ready to hand over at any moment. The machine does both, so people stop doing them by hand at the end.

CI: continuous integration, in systems engineering words

Integration is bringing one person's change into the master copy. Continuous means it happens every day, in small pieces, not in a big merge before a review. Each change is checked automatically before it goes in. In the words you know, CI is a configuration audit plus the peer-review checklist, run by the server on every single change.

For Tidewater, every merge request is checked in a few minutes:

  • Every file is valid SysML v2 text (grammar).
  • Every name points at something that exists (lint).
  • The part tree keeps its shape and level tags (outline).
  • No secret was committed (secrets).
  • Requirements still trace (trace).
  • The generated documents match the model (docs).

CD: continuous delivery

Delivery means producing the products of the model. For Tidewater those are the generated documents, the diagrams, the trace report, the model web site, the release notes and the baselines. Continuous means the pipeline produces them from the model on every merge, so they are always current and ready to hand over. Nobody assembles a delivery package the week before a review. When GitLab talks about deploy, here it only means two things: publishing the model web site (the pages job) and creating a baseline release (the publish-release job).

The anatomy of a pipeline

TermWhat it isTidewater example
pipelineEvery check and product for one change, run by the serverThe pipeline of MR !19
stageA group of jobs that run together. The stages run in order, and a failure stops the later onescheck, then trace, then docs
jobOne check, or one productlint, pages
scriptThe commands a job runs. The job fails if a command failsperl ci/job.pl lint (the job's logic is in that Perl script, so it runs the same in PowerShell, Git Bash or Linux)
runnerThe machine that runs the jobsA Windows PC with Git for Windows (Administration)
rulesWhen a job runs, and when it is skippeddelta runs only for drop branches; baseline only on baseline-* tags
artifactsFiles a job keeps after it ends, for download or for later jobstodo.txt, trace.txt, public/
reportsArtifacts in a format GitLab draws on the merge requestJUnit, Code Quality and metrics from ci-reports.pl
environmentA named place the pipeline delivers to, with a record of what is there nowmodel-site, the Pages site
variablesNamed settings the jobs read. They can be masked and protected for secretsKIT (the kit's path); STATUS_TOKEN (masked)
cacheFiles kept between pipelines to save timeNot needed here: the checks take seconds
allow_failureThe job may fail without blocking the merge. It shows yellowtrace started this way in sprint 3; since sprint 4 it is a ratchet instead
when: manualThe job waits for a person to press its play buttonCould guard a release; Tidewater uses protected tags instead

What starts a pipeline

TriggerWhenWhat runs for Tidewater
merge requestAn MR is opened or updatedThe checks, on the merged result: your branch merged into the current develop, so you test what will actually exist after the merge
pushA branch without an MR changes (develop after a merge, vendor/prime)The checks, pages on develop, delta and drop-package on the vendor branch
tagA baseline-* tag is createdbaseline (the rebuild audit), then publish-release
scheduleA timer, set under Build > Pipeline schedulesstatus, every Friday; the nightly full check (FULL=1) on weekdays

Reading a pipeline and a job log

On the MR page, the pipeline line shows one icon per stage: green is passed, red is failed, yellow is failed but allowed, grey is skipped. Click a red icon, then the red job, to open its log. A log reads top to bottom, like this one with notes added on the right:

Running with gitlab-runner 17.2 on tidewater-win            <- which runner took the job
Fetching changes with git depth set to 0...                 <- the runner gets the merged result
Checking out 3c9e1a2f as detached HEAD (ref is refs/merge-requests/19/merge)
$ perl ci/job.pl lint                                       <- the job's one script line
$ /usr/bin/perl /opt/agile/tools/sysml/model.pl lint        <- what ci/job.pl runs, printed before it runs it
model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml:47:9: error: unresolved type 'Hygrometr'   <- the finding: file, line, column, message
lint: 13 file(s), 1 error(s), 0 warning(s)
elements=139 errors=1 warnings=0                            <- the line the gate reads
$ /usr/bin/perl /opt/agile/tools/gitlab/ci-reports.pl lint --junit lint.xml ...
ci-reports lint: 2 check(s), 2 failed, 1 finding(s); ...    <- reports for the MR widgets
lint is not 0/0 (elements=139 errors=1 warnings=0)          <- why the job failed
Uploading artifacts... lint.txt lint.xml lint-cq.json       <- kept even on failure (when: always)
ERROR: Job failed: exit code 1                              <- a non-zero exit fails the job

The fix is in the line that names a file and a line number. Open it in Vim with vim +47 model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml.

Running it on your own machine first

perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl ci --list --event merge_request_event --branch feature/19-stations --target develop
#   which jobs would run for this MR, and the rule that skips each of the others
perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl ci --event merge_request_event --branch feature/19-stations --target develop --var KIT=$KIT
#   runs them here, stage by stage, with the variables GitLab would set

Shift left: catch it at the merge, not at integration

"Shift left" means moving a check earlier in time, to the left on a schedule chart. An interface mismatch found by lint on the day it was typed costs the author five minutes. The same mismatch found at a design review months later costs a meeting, a defect report and rework of everything built on it. Status metric H counts this directly: the mismatches caught at merge, against those that reached integration.

The Sec in DevSecOps

  • Secret detection on every change: the secrets job and GitLab's own template. A committed token is caught before it is copied into every clone.
  • Protected, masked variables for credentials. A masked variable is hidden in job logs. A protected variable is given only to pipelines on protected branches and tags, so a feature branch cannot read it.
  • A least-privilege runner. The runner gets a normal user account, not an administrator. It is registered to this project only and tagged, so other projects' jobs never run on it. It holds no credentials beyond the job's own token.
  • Least-privilege tokens. Each token gets read_api unless it must write, and an expiry date.
  • Protected branches and tags, so nothing reaches the master copy or a baseline without the pipeline and an approval.

Growing a pipeline one job at a time

Do not write the whole file on day one. Add one job, live with it for a sprint, then add the next. Each job should answer a question a reviewer used to answer by eye.

  1. grammar: is every file valid SysML v2 text?
  2. lint: do all the names resolve? Hold it at 0/0 from the first day.
  3. secrets: is nothing secret committed?
  4. docs: do the generated documents match the model?
  5. trace: do the requirements still trace? Start it as allow_failure, then make it a ratchet (fail only on new gaps).
  6. The reports (JUnit, Code Quality), so failures show on the MR.
  7. pages, baseline, publish-release, and the weekly status.

The minimum pipeline for any SysML v2 text repository

Ten lines, enough to start. Set KIT as a CI/CD variable and copy tools/gitlab/templates/ci/job.pl to ci/job.pl. In the template, the workflow block and the rest come later.

stages:
  - check

grammar:
  stage: check
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl grammar

lint:
  stage: check
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl lint

Why perl ci/job.pl NAME and not shell lines: GitLab Runner's Windows shell executor runs PowerShell, where $KIT is $env:KIT and $(find ...), [ -f ... ], pipes and quoting behave differently. A Perl script behaves the same in PowerShell, cmd, Git Bash, a Linux runner, the Docker image and gitlab.pl ci on a laptop.

The pipeline, job by job

The objection: "We audit at the baseline, like always." Why bother: an audit at the end finds a year of problems at once, when they are hardest to fix. The pipeline is the same configuration audit, written down once and run by the server on every change, in minutes. Problems are found the day they are made, by the person who made them, before they reach the master copy. Nobody spends a week preparing for it.

The pipeline is the part of the process nobody can skip. Each job checks one thing a reviewer would otherwise have to check by eye. Every job's script is one line, perl ci/job.pl NAME; ci/job.pl (committed in the model repo, from tools/gitlab/templates/ci/job.pl) calls the kit through the CI/CD variable KIT. Nothing is installed on the runner beyond Git for Windows (or any Perl 5 with Git).

StageJobRuns onChecksFails the MR?
checkgrammarevery changeEvery .sysml file parses against the official SysML v2 grammaryes
checklintevery changeNames resolve, imports are used; the last line must be errors=0 warnings=0yes
checkoutlineevery change2 to 9 children at every level; each part def has its level tagonly if the change adds a violation (a ratchet against .ci/outline-max)
checktodoevery changeCounts // TODO lines: the port burn-down (artifact todo.txt)never
checksecretsevery changeNo access tokens, cloud keys or private keys in the treeyes
tracetraceevery changeDOORS against the model: linked, orphan, unverified, drifted requirementsonly if the change adds a gap (a ratchet against the merge base); reports only on develop
docsdocsevery changeGenerated docs are committed and currentyes
deltadeltavendor/prime, feature/drop-* MRsWhat the prime changed in v1 since the previous drop; which changes need hand reworkonly on error
releasebaselinetags baseline-*The tagged tree rebuilds its docs byte for byte, the hash matches the tag message; writes toolchain.txt (kit, Perl, Git, OS, runner, image)yes (the tag stays, the release is held)
deltadrop-packagevendor/primeFiles the drop, as delivered, in the generic package registry (prime-drop, by version)only on error
releasepublish-releasetags baseline-*, after baselineCreates the GitLab release with the baseline's CHANGELOG section and the toolchain as notes—
publishpagesthe default branchPublishes the model's web site: generated docs, tree / trace / package views, the trace summary, the TODO burn-downnever blocks a merge (runs after it)
reportstatusthe weekly scheduleExports issues, MRs and jobs for the status metrics—

Words used in the table: a job is one check; a stage is a group of jobs that run together, in the order listed; a runner is the machine that runs them; an artifact is a file a job keeps (a report, a count); a rule says when a job runs.

What the merge request shows: reports

Each check job also writes its results in the formats GitLab draws on the merge request page, using tools/gitlab/ci-reports.pl on the checkers' own output:

ReportShown asWritten byTier
JUnit XML (reports:junit)the test summary: each failed check with its message (one case per model file for grammar and lint; one per requirement gap for trace)ci-reports.pl grammar|lint|outline|trace --junitFree
Code Quality JSON (reports:codequality)the findings this change added or fixed: lint errors and warnings, outline violations, TODO lines (as info)ci-reports.pl ... --codequalityFree (widget), Premium (inline in the diff)
Metrics (reports:metrics)how each number moved against the target branch: todo_lines, lint_errors, trace_completeness_pct, …ci-reports.pl ... --metricsPremium
perl ci/job.pl lint      # runs, in turn:
perl $KIT/tools/sysml/model.pl lint > lint.txt 2>&1
perl $KIT/tools/gitlab/ci-reports.pl lint --junit lint.xml --codequality lint-cq.json --metrics lint.metrics lint.txt
ci-reports lint: 1 check(s), 0 failed, 0 finding(s); model_elements=138 lint_errors=0 lint_warnings=0

A Code Quality finding's fingerprint is a hash of its file, check and message (not its line), so a finding keeps its identity when lines above it move, and GitLab can tell "fixed" from "moved".

Why these rules

  • workflow:rules give one pipeline per change: an MR gets a merge request pipeline, and the same branch does not also get a branch pipeline. Without it every push to an MR runs twice.
  • The trace job is a ratchet. Requirement gaps are often the prime's to fix (a discrepancy report); blocking every unrelated MR on them would stop the team without fixing anything. So on a merge request the job also traces the model as it was at the merge base, and fails only when the change adds a gap: removes a satisfy, drops a verify, edits a requirement's text away from DOORS. The existing gaps stay in the widget.
  • Hidden jobs and anchors (.check, &model_rules) keep the shared rules in one place: the weekly status schedule runs only the report; the nightly schedule (FULL=1) runs the full check and refreshes the site.
  • include: template: Security/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml adds GitLab's own secret scanner, but only when the project variable DOCKER_RUNNER is "true" (the include has its own rules:). The scanner runs in a Docker image; on the team's Windows shell runner its job would wait forever and, with "pipelines must succeed", block every MR. The secrets job is the always-on check: a scan of every tracked file in ci/job.pl, which runs on any runner and on a laptop.
  • default: tags: [windows, mbse] sends the jobs to the team's Windows shell runner. On a Docker runner (tools/gitlab/docker) drop the tags or use that runner's own.
  • The outline job is a ratchet. The converted model inherits outline violations from the prime's structure, most of them fixable only upstream. .ci/outline-max holds the count allowed: a change that adds a violation fails; a change that removes one lowers the number in the same MR. At 0 the rule is absolute.
# .gitlab-ci.yml -- the Tidewater government model pipeline (tools/gitlab/templates/gitlab-ci.yml).
#
# In configuration-management terms this file is the CONFIGURATION AUDIT, written down once and run by the server on
# every proposed change (every merge request), on every baseline tag, nightly and once a week for the status report.
# A job is one audit check; a stage is a group of checks that run together; the stages run in the order listed below.
#
# Copy it to the model repo as .gitlab-ci.yml, with tools/gitlab/templates/ci/job.pl as ci/job.pl. Every job's script
# is one line, `perl ci/job.pl NAME`: the job's logic lives in that Perl script, so it runs the same under the Windows
# runner's PowerShell, cmd, Git Bash, a Linux runner, the Docker image (tools/gitlab/docker) and `gitlab.pl ci` on a
# laptop. ci/job.pl calls the agile kit through the CI/CD variable KIT (the path of the kit's checkout on the runner;
# `gitlab.pl setup` sets it from project.conf [variables]). Nothing is installed: Perl and Git are all a job needs.
#
# Run it on your own machine before you push, with the same rules GitLab applies:
#   perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl ci --event merge_request_event --branch feature/12-stations --target develop --var KIT=$KIT
#   perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl ci --list            (which jobs would run, and why the others are skipped)
#
# Stages, in order:
#   check    the gate: grammar, structure lint, outline (a ratchet), secrets, and the TODO count (the port burn-down)
#   trace    DOORS against the model (a ratchet on merge requests); the VCRM; SIL/HIL when a harness exists (disabled)
#   docs     generated docs must be committed and current
#   delta    on drop intake only: the delivery checked (intake, on a trigger), what the prime changed in v1 (delta),
#            and the drop filed in the package registry
#   release  on baseline tags only: the baseline rebuilds byte for byte, then the GitLab release is created
#   publish  on the default branch only: the model's web site (GitLab Pages) for readers who never open the repo
#   report   on the weekly schedule only: export issues, MRs and jobs for the status metrics
#
# Reports: the check jobs attach JUnit (the MR's test widget: which check failed and why), Code Quality (the MR's
# findings widget: which errors, warnings or TODO lines this change added or fixed) and metrics (Premium: how each
# number moved) -- all written by $KIT/tools/gitlab/ci-reports.pl from the checkers' own output, called by ci/job.pl.
#
# YAML note: a script line that contains ": " (colon, space) must be in quotes, or YAML reads it as a map. With
# ci/job.pl there are none left.

stages:
  - check
  - trace
  - docs
  - delta
  - release
  - publish
  - report

variables:
  GIT_DEPTH: "0"            # the full history: trace reads the merge base, delta reads earlier imports, pages the merges

# One pipeline per change, never two: an MR gets a merge request pipeline; a branch with an open MR does not also get a
# branch pipeline. Branches without an MR (develop, main, vendor/prime), tags and the schedules still get theirs.
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS && $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "push"'
      when: never
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_TAG'
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"'

# GitLab's own secret scanner (Free tier) runs its analyzer in a Docker image, so it needs a runner with the Docker
# executor. The team's runner is a Windows *shell* runner: there the scanner's job would sit "pending" forever and, with
# "pipelines must succeed", block every MR. So the include is conditional: it is pulled in only when the project
# variable DOCKER_RUNNER is "true" (project.conf [variables] sets it to "false"). The `secrets` job below is the
# always-on check, runnable on any runner and by `gitlab.pl ci` on a laptop (which lists the include as "runs on
# GitLab only").
include:
  - template: Security/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml
    rules:
      - if: '$DOCKER_RUNNER == "true"'

# Runner tags pick the runner: the team's Windows shell runner is registered with the tags windows and mbse. On a
# Docker runner (tools/gitlab/docker), drop these tags or use that runner's own.
default:
  tags:
    - windows
    - mbse

# The rules every model job shares: run on changes and on the nightly full check (FULL=1), never on the weekly status
# schedule (that one only reports) or a delivery trigger (that one only takes the drop in).
.model_rules: &model_rules
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule" && $FULL != "1"'
      when: never
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "trigger"'
      when: never
    # vendor/prime holds the prime's drop as delivered, converted and untouched: the model checks run where it is
    # merged (feature/drop-VERSION and its MR), not on the raw branch, which would stay red (no docs, no recorded
    # outline count) for structure only the prime can change. The delta and drop-package jobs still run there.
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "vendor/prime"'
      when: never
    - when: on_success

# A hidden job: the check-stage jobs extend it. Reports are kept even when the check fails (that is when they matter).
.check:
  stage: check
  <<: *model_rules

# GRAMMAR -- every .sysml file against the official SysML v2 grammar (tools/sysml/sysml.pl, built from the vendored
# KerML/SysML release). A syntax error anywhere stops the merge. One JUnit test case per file.
grammar:
  extends: .check
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl grammar
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - grammar.txt
    reports:
      junit: grammar.xml
      codequality: grammar-cq.json

# LINT -- the model's structure: names resolve, packages import what they use. The last line is
# elements=N errors=E warnings=W; the gate is 0 errors and 0 warnings ("0/0 to merge").
lint:
  extends: .check
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl lint
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - lint.txt
    reports:
      junit: lint.xml
      codequality: lint-cq.json
      metrics: lint.metrics

# OUTLINE -- 2 to 9 children at every level, and each part def carries its level tag (@L1Network ... @L6Component).
# A RATCHET, not a wall: the converted v1 model starts with violations it inherited from the prime's structure (a
# 25-member package, parts with one child), and most can only be fixed upstream, by a discrepancy report to the prime.
# So the gate is "no new violations": .ci/outline-max holds the highest count allowed; a change that adds a violation
# fails, a change that removes one is told to lower the number (and the reviewer checks that it did). When the count
# reaches 0 the file reads 0 and the rule is absolute. A new project (kickoff.pl scaffold) starts with room: its
# skeleton's one-file folders plus one for each layer folder still to come, with comment lines saying when to tighten
# it (every layer folder holds two files, or the first baseline at the latest); the job reads only the first line.
outline:
  extends: .check
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl outline
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - outline.txt
    reports:
      junit: outline.xml
      codequality: outline-cq.json
      metrics: outline.metrics

# TODO -- the port burn-down: every // TODO line the converter left. Never fails. Each TODO is an "info" finding, so the
# MR widget shows the TODO lines a change closed (and any it added).
todo:
  extends: .check
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl todo
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - todo.txt
    reports:
      codequality: todo-cq.json
      metrics: todo.metrics

# SECRETS -- tokens, cloud keys and private keys must never reach the repo (an MR is the last place to catch it).
secrets:
  extends: .check
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl secrets

# COMPLEXITY -- the spider-web guardrails: per package fan-in and fan-out, dependency cycles, dependencies that go up the
# layers named in sysml.conf (`layers = ...`, lowest first), duplicate names, and relationship ends per part def (the
# spaghetti measure). A RATCHET on merge requests: it fails only when a change makes a measure worse than on the target
# branch, or adds a wildcard import to a government file. Findings show in the MR's Code Quality widget.
complexity:
  extends: .check
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl complexity
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - complexity.txt
    reports:
      codequality: complexity-cq.json
      metrics: complexity.metrics

# TRACE -- DOORS against the model, from the newest imported drop: linked (C), orphans (F), unverified (G), text drift.
# A RATCHET on merge requests: the job also traces the model as it was at the merge base and fails only when this change
# adds a gap (removes a satisfy, drops a verify, edits a requirement's text away from DOORS). Gaps the prime must fix
# stay visible in the widget without blocking unrelated work. On develop and schedules it reports and passes.
trace:
  stage: trace
  <<: *model_rules
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl trace
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - trace.txt
    reports:
      junit: trace.xml
      metrics: trace.metrics

# VCRM -- the verification cross-reference matrix: every requirement, its verification method, the cases that verify it
# (verify relationships in the model) and their newest verdicts from verification/*.csv (one schema: requirement, case,
# verdict, commit, environment, timestamp, signed_by -- the prime's test results ride in each drop from drop 4 on;
# analysis and inspection verdicts are entered and signed by a person). Reports, never blocks: the trace ratchet gates
# missing cases. vcrm.html is also on the Pages site.
vcrm:
  stage: trace
  <<: *model_rules
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl vcrm
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - vcrm.html
      - vcrm.csv
    reports:
      junit: vcrm.xml
      metrics: vcrm.metrics

# RECIPE -- every requirement statement graded against the requirement recipe (tools/sysml/req-recipe.pl): missing
# parts, weak verbs ("provide", "support"), passive voice, vague words. Reports only: the DOORS text is the prime's,
# so findings go to the prime as a discrepancy report. Findings show in the MR's Code Quality widget.
recipe:
  stage: trace
  <<: *model_rules
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl recipe
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - recipe.txt
    reports:
      codequality: recipe-cq.json
      metrics: recipe.metrics

# DOCS -- generated docs (docs/Nouns.md, Verbs.md, idef0/, Traceability.md) are committed with the model that made them.
# Stale docs fail here: run model.pl docs and commit the result.
docs:
  stage: docs
  <<: *model_rules
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl docs

# DELTA -- drop intake: the v1 delta between the two newest imports. Runs on the vendor branch and on the drop merge MR,
# so the reviewer sees what the prime changed, including what the converter cannot carry (state machines, interactions,
# constraint expressions), which has to be reworked by hand.
delta:
  stage: delta
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME =~ /^feature\/drop-/'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "vendor/prime"'
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl delta
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - delta.txt

# DROP-PACKAGE -- file each prime drop, exactly as delivered, in the project's Generic Package Registry
# (Deploy > Package registry > prime-drop): the CDRL deliverable kept with the model it became, downloadable by version.
# The job token authenticates; nothing to configure. Skipped outside GitLab (no registry on a laptop).
drop-package:
  stage: delta
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "vendor/prime"'
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl drop-package

# INTAKE -- a delivery from the prime's Jenkins: its build uploads the drop to the Generic Package Registry (prime-drop/
# <version>, with a deploy token that can do nothing else) and fires a pipeline trigger with DROP_VERSION. This job then
# fetches every file, checks each sha256 against the MANIFEST the prime's build wrote, keeps the drop as received
# (formal evidence: never expires) and opens the Prime Drop issue that starts the vendor import. A green Jenkins build
# on the prime's side is evidence, not acceptance: the government's own gates run on the import MR.
intake:
  stage: delta
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "trigger" && $DROP_VERSION'
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl intake
  artifacts:
    expire_in: never
    paths:
      - intake.txt
      - intake/

# BASELINE -- a baseline tag must rebuild: regenerate the docs, confirm nothing changed, and check the hash in the tag
# message: sha256 over `git ls-tree -r <commit> -- docs` (mode, blob id and path of every tracked file under docs/),
# the same text `gitlab.pl flow released` hashed when it wrote the tag. It also writes toolchain.txt: the kit version,
# Perl, Git, OS, runner and image that produced the baseline (an inventory for the audit). This is the physical
# configuration audit of the baseline, done by machine.
baseline:
  stage: release
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^baseline-/'
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl baseline
  artifacts:
    expire_in: never         # formal evidence: the baseline's audit, toolchain and VCRM are kept for the life of the program
    paths:
      - toolchain.txt
      - vcrm.html
      - vcrm.csv
    reports:
      dotenv: release.env    # RELEASE_MILESTONE: the sprint this baseline closes, for the release below

# PUBLISH-PACKAGE -- the baseline as a package for downstream users (other programs, the test range, the prime): the
# model and its docs at the tag (git archive), the VCRM, the toolchain and SHA256SUMS, as tidewater-model/<tag> in the
# Generic Package Registry. CI_JOB_TOKEN authenticates the upload. The release below links to these files.
publish-package:
  stage: release
  needs:
    - baseline
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^baseline-/'
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl publish-package
  artifacts:
    expire_in: never
    paths:
      - package-upload/

# PUBLISH-RELEASE -- once the baseline audit passes, create the GitLab release for the tag (Deploy > Releases), with the
# baseline's CHANGELOG section, its verification summary and the toolchain as notes, links to the package files, and
# the sprint milestone it closes (GitLab then collects the release evidence: the milestone's issues and the tag
# pipeline's test report, as a JSON snapshot). The `release:` keyword is run by GitLab's release-cli after the script.
publish-release:
  stage: release
  needs:
    - baseline
    - publish-package
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^baseline-/'
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl publish-release
  release:
    tag_name: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
    name: 'Tidewater model $CI_COMMIT_TAG'
    description: release-notes.md
    milestones:
      - $RELEASE_MILESTONE
    assets:
      links:
        - name: 'Model and docs (tar.gz)'
          url: '${CI_API_V4_URL}/projects/${CI_PROJECT_ID}/packages/generic/tidewater-model/${CI_COMMIT_TAG}/tidewater-model-${CI_COMMIT_TAG}.tar.gz'
          link_type: package
        - name: 'VCRM (csv)'
          url: '${CI_API_V4_URL}/projects/${CI_PROJECT_ID}/packages/generic/tidewater-model/${CI_COMMIT_TAG}/vcrm.csv'
          link_type: other
        - name: 'Toolchain'
          url: '${CI_API_V4_URL}/projects/${CI_PROJECT_ID}/packages/generic/tidewater-model/${CI_COMMIT_TAG}/toolchain.txt'
          link_type: other
        - name: 'SHA256SUMS'
          url: '${CI_API_V4_URL}/projects/${CI_PROJECT_ID}/packages/generic/tidewater-model/${CI_COMMIT_TAG}/SHA256SUMS'
          link_type: other

# SIL / HIL -- software-in-the-loop regression (nightly) and hardware-in-the-loop tests (on a bench, by hand), for when
# the program has a simulation or a lab to drive. DISABLED: each runs only when its variable is "true" (SIL_ENABLED,
# HIL_ENABLED), so this file stays valid where there is no harness. Each job runs the harness named by SIL_CMD /
# HIL_CMD and files its verdicts in the same results schema (verification/results-sil.csv / -hil.csv), so the VCRM
# shows them next to the prime's results. The HIL job shows the GitLab features a lab needs: a runner tag that only the
# bench's runner has, a resource_group (one test on the bench at a time), when: manual (a person starts it, with the
# bench ready), and an environment (the bench's deployment history).
sil-regression:
  stage: trace
  rules:
    - if: '$SIL_ENABLED == "true" && $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"'
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl sil-regression
  artifacts:
    expire_in: never
    paths:
      - sil.txt
      - verification/results-sil.csv

hil-test:
  stage: trace
  tags:
    - hil-bench
  resource_group: hil-bench
  rules:
    - if: '$HIL_ENABLED == "true" && $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH'
      when: manual
  environment:
    name: hil-lab
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl hil-test
  artifacts:
    expire_in: never
    paths:
      - hil.txt
      - verification/results-hil.csv

# PAGES -- the model's web site, rebuilt on every merge to the default branch and nightly: the generated docs, the tree /
# trace / package views, the requirement trace and the port burn-down. For the program office, the prime and review
# boards: people who need the model's state and will never clone a repository. GitLab serves public/ at $CI_PAGES_URL.
pages:
  stage: publish
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule" && $FULL != "1"'
      when: never
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "trigger"'
      when: never
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH'
  environment:
    name: model-site
    url: $CI_PAGES_URL
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl pages
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - public

# STATUS -- weekly, from a pipeline schedule (Build > Pipeline schedules, Fridays 06:00): export what GitLab knows --
# issues, MRs, jobs -- in the status-metrics formats, and collect this week's metrics if the repo has a metrics.json.
# STATUS_TOKEN is a masked CI/CD variable holding a read_api project access token.
status:
  stage: report
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule" && $FULL != "1"'
  script:
    - perl ci/job.pl status
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - exports/

And the script every job runs, ci/job.pl:

#!/usr/bin/perl
# ci/job.pl -- every job of the model pipeline, in core Perl, so .gitlab-ci.yml only ever says `perl ci/job.pl NAME`.
#
# Why a script and not shell lines in the YAML: GitLab Runner's Windows shell executor runs PowerShell, where $KIT is
# $env:KIT and `$(find ...)`, `[ -f ... ]`, `| xargs`, `&&` and quoting all differ from sh. One Perl script behaves the
# same under PowerShell, cmd, Git Bash, a Linux runner, the Docker image and `gitlab.pl ci` on a laptop. The YAML keeps
# what GitLab needs to know (when a job runs, what it keeps, which reports it attaches); this file keeps what it does.
#
#   perl ci/job.pl grammar | lint | outline | todo | secrets | trace | vcrm | docs | delta | drop-package | intake | baseline
#                  | publish-package | publish-release | pages | status | sil-regression | hil-test
#
# Every job needs the CI/CD variable KIT (the agile kit's checkout on the runner) and writes its log and report files
# in the project directory: NAME.txt (the checker's own output), NAME.xml (JUnit), NAME-cq.json (Code Quality),
# NAME.metrics (metrics), via $KIT/tools/gitlab/ci-reports.pl. Exit status: 0 pass, 1 the check failed, 2 the job
# cannot run (KIT missing, bad usage).
#
# Copied into the model repository as ci/job.pl (from tools/gitlab/templates/ci/job.pl). Core Perl only.
package CIJob;                                # a package, so tests can `require` this file and call its functions
use strict;
use warnings;
use File::Find ();
use File::Path qw(make_path);
use File::Copy qw(copy);
use Digest::SHA ();

my %JOBS = map { $_ => 1 } qw(grammar lint outline todo secrets trace vcrm recipe complexity docs delta drop-package intake baseline publish-package
                                publish-release pages status sil-regression hil-test);
our $KIT = $ENV{KIT} // '';
# The toolchain is pinned like the model: .kit-version names the kit release the model was checked with. A runner with a
# different kit fails every job, so a tool upgrade reaches the model only through a reviewed MR that bumps the pin.
sub kit_version { my $v = $ENV{KIT_VERSION}; return $v if defined $v && length $v;
    my $o = `git -C "$KIT" describe --tags --always 2>&1`; $o =~ s/\s+$//; $? ? 'unknown' : $o }
sub main {
    my $job = shift // '';
    if (!$JOBS{$job}) { print STDERR "usage: perl ci/job.pl " . join(' | ', sort keys %JOBS) . "\n"; return 2 }
    if ($KIT eq '') { print STDERR "KIT is not set: add it under Settings > CI/CD > Variables (the kit's path on the runner)\n"; return 2 }
    if (!-f "$KIT/tools/sysml/model.pl") { print STDERR "KIT=$KIT does not hold the agile kit (no tools/sysml/model.pl)\n"; return 2 }
    $| = 1;
    if (open my $pin, '<', '.kit-version') {
        my $want = <$pin> // ''; close $pin;
        $want =~ s/^\s+|\s+$//g;
        my $have = kit_version();
        if (length $want && $want ne $have) {
            print STDERR "the kit on this runner is $have, but .kit-version pins $want:\n"
                       . "  bump .kit-version in a merge request (toolchain changes are reviewed like model changes), or put the runner back on $want\n";
            return 2;
        }
    }
    our %run;
    $run{$job}->() ? 1 : 0;
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- helpers
sub slurp { my $f = shift; open my $fh, '<:raw', $f or return undef; local $/; my $t = <$fh>; close $fh; $t // '' }
sub spew { my ($f, $t) = @_; open my $fh, '>:raw', $f or die "cannot write $f: $!\n"; print $fh $t; close $fh }
our $QUIET = 0;                               # local $QUIET = 1: run() writes the log file only, not the job log
sub run {                                     # run(LOGFILE|undef, cmd...) -> exit code; output (stdout+stderr) to the log and the job log
    my ($log, @cmd) = @_;
    print '$ ', join(' ', map { /\s/ ? "\"$_\"" : $_ } @cmd), "\n" unless $QUIET;
    return system(@cmd) >> 8 unless defined $log;
    open my $save_out, '>&', \*STDOUT or die "cannot save STDOUT: $!\n";
    open my $save_err, '>&', \*STDERR or die "cannot save STDERR: $!\n";
    open STDOUT, '>', $log or die "cannot write $log: $!\n";
    open STDERR, '>&', \*STDOUT or die "cannot redirect STDERR: $!\n";
    my $rc = system(@cmd);
    open STDOUT, '>&', $save_out or die "cannot restore STDOUT: $!\n";
    open STDERR, '>&', $save_err or die "cannot restore STDERR: $!\n";
    print slurp($log) // '' unless $QUIET;
    $rc == -1 ? 127 : $rc >> 8;
}
sub out {                                     # out(cmd...) -> its standard output (a temp file, not a pipe: list-form pipes are not portable)
    my @cmd = @_;
    require File::Temp;
    my ($fh, $tmp) = File::Temp::tempfile('ci-job-XXXXXX', TMPDIR => 1, UNLINK => 1);
    close $fh;
    open my $save, '>&', \*STDOUT or die "cannot save STDOUT: $!\n";
    open STDOUT, '>', $tmp or die "cannot write $tmp: $!\n";
    system(@cmd);
    open STDOUT, '>&', $save or die "cannot restore STDOUT: $!\n";
    my $t = slurp($tmp) // '';
    unlink $tmp;
    $t;
}
sub perl_tool { my ($log, $tool, @args) = @_; run($log, $^X, "$KIT/$tool", @args) }
sub reports { my ($mode, @args) = @_; perl_tool(undef, 'tools/gitlab/ci-reports.pl', $mode, @args) }
sub sysml_files { my @f; File::Find::find({ no_chdir => 1, wanted => sub { push @f, $File::Find::name if /\.sysml$/ && -f } }, 'model') if -d 'model'; sort @f }
sub vkey { my $v = shift; join '.', map { /^\d+$/ ? sprintf('%06d', $_) : $_ } split /[.\-]/, $v }
sub imports {                                 # the imported prime drops, oldest first (imports/v1.0, imports/v1.1, ... in version order)
    opendir my $dh, 'imports' or return ();
    my @d = grep { !/^\./ && -d "imports/$_" } readdir $dh;
    closedir $dh;
    map { "imports/$_" } sort { vkey($a) cmp vkey($b) } @d;
}
sub ls { my $d = shift; opendir(my $dh, $d) or return (); my @e = sort grep { !/^\./ } readdir $dh; closedir $dh; @e }
sub docs_hash { Digest::SHA::sha256_hex(out('git', 'ls-tree', '-r', $_[0] // 'HEAD', '--', 'docs')) }   # the same text GitFlow hashes
sub sha256_file { my $f = shift; my $d = Digest::SHA->new(256); open my $fh, '<:raw', $f or return ''; $d->addfile($fh); close $fh; $d->hexdigest }
sub last_line { my $t = shift // ''; my @l = grep { /\S/ } split /\n/, $t; $l[-1] // '' }

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- the jobs
our %run;
$run{grammar} = sub {                         # every .sysml file against the SysML v2 grammar; one JUnit case per file
    my @f = sysml_files();
    if (!@f) { spew('grammar.txt', "no .sysml files under model/\n"); print "no .sysml files under model/ yet\n"; return 0 }
    my $rc = perl_tool('grammar.txt', 'tools/sysml/sysml.pl', 'check', @f);
    reports('grammar', '--junit', 'grammar.xml', '--codequality', 'grammar-cq.json', 'grammar.txt', @f);
    $rc;
};
$run{lint} = sub {                            # structure: the gate is 0 errors and 0 warnings
    perl_tool('lint.txt', 'tools/sysml/model.pl', 'lint');
    reports('lint', '--junit', 'lint.xml', '--codequality', 'lint-cq.json', '--metrics', 'lint.metrics', 'lint.txt');
    my $l = last_line(slurp('lint.txt'));
    return 0 if $l =~ / errors=0 warnings=0$/;
    print "lint is not 0/0 ($l)\n";
    1;
};
sub outline_junit_inherited {                 # findings the allowance already covers: skipped tests, not failures (a green MR shows no red)
    my $x = slurp('outline.xml') // return;
    my $n = $x =~ s{<failure message="([^"]*)"[^>]*>.*?</failure>}{<skipped message="inherited, within .ci/outline-max: $1"/>}gs;
    return unless $n;
    $x =~ s{(<testsuites?\b[^>]*?) failures="(\d+)"}{my ($h, $f) = ($1, $2); "$h failures=\"0\" skipped=\"$f\""}ge;
    spew('outline.xml', $x);
}
$run{outline} = sub {                         # the 2..9 rule and level tags, as a ratchet against .ci/outline-max
    perl_tool('outline.txt', 'tools/sysml/model.pl', 'check');
    reports('outline', '--junit', 'outline.xml', '--codequality', 'outline-cq.json', '--metrics', 'outline.metrics', 'outline.txt');
    my $t = slurp('outline.txt');
    my ($v) = $t =~ /^violations\s+(\d+)/m;
    my ($m) = $t =~ /^\@L tag mismatches\s+(\d+)/m;
    my $n = ($v // 0) + ($m // 0);
    my $file = slurp('.ci/outline-max') // '';
    my $max = $file =~ /^\s*(\d+)/ ? $1 : 0;   # the first line; comment lines after it (a new scaffold's room) are for people
    print "outline violations: $n (allowed: $max)\n";
    # vendor/prime holds the prime's structure as delivered, and a drop branch merges it: measured, not ratcheted (the
    # drop's merge request records the new count in .ci/outline-max; Discrepancy Reports ask the prime to fix the rest)
    if (($ENV{CI_COMMIT_BRANCH} // '') =~ m{^(?:vendor/prime$|feature/drop-)} || ($ENV{CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME} // '') =~ m{^feature/drop-}) {   # the MR and the branch's own pushes
        outline_junit_inherited();
        print "a prime drop: reported, not ratcheted\n";
        return 0;
    }
    if (($ENV{CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME} // '') =~ m{^release/} || ($ENV{CI_COMMIT_BRANCH} // '') =~ m{^release/}) {   # as complexity: develop already checked it
        outline_junit_inherited();
        print "a release: its changes were checked on develop; reported only\n";
        return 0;
    }
    if ($n > $max) { print "this change adds outline violations ($n > $max): fix them, do not raise .ci/outline-max\n"; return 1 }
    if ($n < $max) {                       # a scaffold's allowance keeps room for new one-file folders until its comment says to tighten it
        print $file =~ /^#/m ? "fewer violations than allowed: room left for new folders (see the comment in .ci/outline-max for when to tighten it to $n)\n"
                             : "fewer violations than allowed: lower .ci/outline-max to $n in this MR\n";
    }
    outline_junit_inherited();
    0;
};
$run{todo} = sub {                            # the port burn-down: every // TODO line the converter left; never fails
    my @hits;
    for my $f (sysml_files()) { my $n = 0; for my $l (split /\n/, slurp($f)) { $n++; push @hits, "$f:$n:$l" if index($l, '// TODO') >= 0 } }
    spew('todo.txt', join('', map { "$_\n" } @hits));
    print "TODO lines remaining: " . scalar(@hits) . "\n";
    reports('todo', '--codequality', 'todo-cq.json', '--metrics', 'todo.metrics', -d 'model' ? 'model' : 'todo.txt');
    0;
};
$run{secrets} = sub {                         # tokens, cloud keys and private keys must never reach the repository
    my @pat = (qr/glpat-[0-9A-Za-z_\-]{20}/, qr/AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}/, qr/-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----/);
    my @bad;
    for my $f (grep { length } split /\n/, out('git', 'ls-files')) {
        next if $f eq '.gitlab-ci.yml' || $f eq 'ci/job.pl';
        my $t = slurp($f) // next;
        next if $t =~ /\x00/;                 # binary
        my $n = 0;
        for my $l (split /\n/, $t) { $n++; for my $p (@pat) { push @bad, "$f:$n: matches $p" if $l =~ $p } }
    }
    if (@bad) { print "$_\n" for @bad; print "possible secret committed: remove it, rotate it, then rewrite the branch before it merges\n"; return 1 }
    print "no secrets found in " . scalar(grep { length } split /\n/, out('git', 'ls-files')) . " tracked files\n";
    0;
};
